Twelve-tone writing: one row, many phrases
Rhythm: two beats can become three
Orchestration: the flute hands over its tune
Spectralism: an ensemble inside a low E
Sonata form presents themes in different keys, develops them, then brings them back around the home key.
An exposition introduces the main themes of a sonata-form movement or the first round of subject entries in a fugue.
The development is the middle section of a sonata-form movement, where earlier themes are altered and taken through other keys.
The recapitulation brings back a sonata-form movement’s opening themes, usually with the later themes now in the home key.
A coda is a closing passage added after a piece’s main sections, ranging from a few chords to a substantial final section.
A rondo brings its main tune back between contrasting episodes, often in the pattern A–B–A–C–A.
Ternary form has an opening section, a contrasting middle and a return of the opening, often with changes.
Binary form divides a piece into two main sections, usually repeated, with the second bringing the music home.
Theme and variations presents a tune followed by altered versions that retain something of its melody, bass or chords.
A fugue builds a piece from a theme that enters in successive voices and returns throughout the music.
